title.en: The Oriole That Sings for Kim

texts.period: Folk legends of birds collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 3 'The Rabbit and other Legends', eBook #55539

summary.en: One of the numerous ladies at court once had a love affair with a palace official, a Mr. Kim. It was discovered and the poor thing lost her life; but her spirit could not be killed, and unappeased it entered the oriole, in which form she returned to the palace singing 'Kim-pul-lah-go', 'tell Kim to come', and, receiving no response, mournfully entreating 'Kim-poh-go-sip-so', 'I want to see Kim'. Even to this day the women and children feel sad when they hear these plaintive notes, and their hearts go out in pity for the poor lone lover ever searching in vain for her Kim.
summary.zh: 相傳宮中嬪御與內官金某私通，事泄被誅。其魂不滅，附於黃鳥，飛回宮中，啼曰『金不喇高』（喚金），無應，復哀鳴『金潑高息潑』（思見金）。至今婦孺聞此鳥聲，無不感傷。

passages.text: Once upon a time, one of the numerous ladies at court had a love affair with one of the palace officials, a Mr. Kim. It was discovered, and the poor thing lost her life. Her spirit could not be killed, however, and, unappeased, it entered this bird, in which form she returned to the palace.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 3 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: She sang, 'Kim-pul-lah-go' — 'tell Kim to come' — and then, receiving no response, would mournfully entreat, 'Kim-poh-go-sip-so' — 'I want to see Kim.' So, even to this day, the women and children feel sad when they hear these plaintive notes, and unconsciously their hearts go out in pity for the poor lone lover who is ever searching in vain for her Kim.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 3 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: The Magpie's News and the Goose of Constancy

texts.period: Folk legends of birds collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 3, eBook #55539

summary.en: The magpie is in great favor in Korea: should he come to the house with his song in the morning, good news may be expected during the day — father returning from a long journey, a brother succeeding in his examination; in the afternoon, a guest may be expected with an appetite equal to a family of children; after dark, thieves may be dreaded. He is also champion of the swallows, dashing at the head of the house-snake that has eaten their young. The wild goose participates in every wedding ceremony, for these observing people once noticed that a goose whose mate was killed returned year after year to mourn her loss, and such constancy they seek to commend to their wives, pledging each other: 'Black is the hair that now crowns our heads, yet when it has become as white as the fibres of the onion root, we shall still be found faithful to each other.'
summary.zh: 朝鮮人最喜鵲。晨鵲鳴於門，是日必有喜事：或遠人歸，或子弟登科；午則有客至；暮則防盜。鵲又為燕之友，啄食蛇頭以護雛。雁則婚礼必用之，以雁失偶後歲歲哀鳴，取其貞也。夫婦交拜時互誓云：『今結髮皆黑，他年皓首，此心如雁不改。』

sensitivity.note: Bird-omen and wedding-custom etiology; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The magpie, that impudent, noisy nuisance, is in great favor, so much so that his great ugly nest is safe from human disturbance. When one of the great lazy house-snakes comes out to sun himself after a meal of young swallows, the bereaved parents fly off for the saucy magpie, who comes promptly and dashes at the snake's head amid the encouraging jabbering of the swallows.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 3 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: Should the magpie come to the house with his song in the morning, good news may be expected during the day: father will return from a long journey; brother will succeed in his examination and obtain rank. Should the magpie come in the afternoon, a guest may be expected with an appetite equal to that of a family of children; while, if the magpie comes after dark, thieves may be dreaded.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 3 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: The wild goose is one of the most highly prized birds in Korea. It always participates in the wedding ceremonies; for no man would think himself properly married had he not been presented by his bride with a wild goose. The reason is that these observing people once noticed that a goose whose mate was killed returned to the place year after year to mourn her loss; and such constancy they seek, by this pretty custom, to commend to their wives. They further pledge each other at this time: 'Black is the hair that now crowns our heads, yet when it has become as white as the fibres of the onion root, we shall still be found faithful to each other.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 3 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: The White Heron Who Pecked the Temple Bell

texts.period: Folk legends of birds collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 3, eBook #55539

summary.en: The white heron is the especial friend of man. Many are the tales told of the assistance it has rendered: in one case the generous-hearted creature is said to have pecked off its bill in its frantic attempts to ring a temple bell for the salvation of a man. In another, a hunter who shot an arrow through the head of a snake about to devour some newly hatched herons was in turn saved by the mother bird, who pecked to death a snake that had gotten into the man's stomach while he was drinking at a spring — the pecking so expertly done as not to injure the man.
summary.zh: 白鶴為人之友。相傳曾自啄其喙，以撞寺鐘而活一人。又一獵者射蛇以救雛鶴，後鶴母啄出其腹中之蛇，毫髮無傷，以報其恩。

passages.text: The white heron seems to be the especial friend of man. Many are the tales told of the assistance it has rendered individuals: in one case the generous-hearted creature is said to have pecked off its bill in its frantic attempts to ring a temple bell for the salvation of a man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 3 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: One of the early stories relates how a hunter, having shot an arrow through the head of a snake that was about to devour some newly hatched herons, was in turn saved by the mother bird, who pecked to death a snake that had gotten into the man's stomach while he was drinking at a spring — the pecking, further, was so expertly done as not to injure the man.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 3 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: The Rabbit Who Kept Both His Eyes

region.en: Undersea palace of the fish-king (symbolic pin)

texts.period: Animal folktale collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 3 'The Rabbit and other Legends', eBook #55539

summary.en: The king of fishes gets a hook through his nose and grows very ill; in solemn council the turtle declares that a poultice made from the fresh eye of a rabbit would cure him, and undertakes to bring one up from the beach. Feigning that the view from the hills is nothing to the sights of the undersea world, the turtle lures the curious rabbit onto his back and carries him down to the palace, where the doctors explain the plot of securing his eyes before he should die. The rabbit saves himself with a happy thought: he always carries two pairs of eyes, real ones and a pair of mountain crystal for dusty weather — and fearing the water would injure the real ones, he buried them in the sand before mounting. Let him ride back and dig them up. Marvelling at the rabbit's courtesy, the fishes are ashamed; once released on the sand, the rabbit shakes the water from his coat, winks at his clumsy betrayer, tells him to dig for the eyes himself, and tears away up the mountainside, ever after giving the turtle a wide berth.
summary.zh: 魚王誤吞魚鉤，群醫束手。老龜獻策：以兔眼為膏藥可治，遂上山誘兔曰『海底之勝過於山巔』。兔好奇，伏龜背而入海。至龍宮，醫者密議於兔死之前取其目。兔聞之大恐，詭言『吾有二目，真目畏水，已埋於沙，今所用者水晶目也。願歸取一目以奉大王』。魚眾愧其詐而放之。兔登岸大笑，令龜自掘，遂遁入山，終身避龜。

sensitivity.note: Animal trickster tale; parallels the Tortoise-and-Hare and Brer Rabbit types and the Dragon Palace visit (cf. Urashima).

passages.text: The king of fishes, while snapping greedily at a worm, got a hook through his nose. He succeeded in breaking the line, but he could in no way remove the cruel hook, and his finny majesty grew very ill; all the officials of his kingdom were summoned and met in solemn council. At last the turtle announced his firm belief that a poultice made from the fresh eye of a rabbit would remove the disorder of their sovereign at once.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 3 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: The turtle concealed his excitement under an air of indifference, boasting of the magnificent sights under the water, and offered to carry the rabbit down on his back. The rabbit was charmed and bewildered by the magnificence of everything he saw, and especially by the gorgeous palace, through which he was escorted to the sick chamber of the king. While sitting in an elegant chair he chanced to hear a discussion concerning the best way of securing his eyes before he should die; questioning an attendant, the whole plot was explained to him. The poor fellow scratched his head and wondered if he would ever get out of the place alive.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 3 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: At last a happy thought struck him. He explained that he always carried about two pairs of eyes, his real ones and a pair made of mountain crystals to be used in dusty weather; fearing that the water would injure his real eyes, he had buried them in the sand before getting upon the turtle's back, and was now using his crystal ones. He was most willing to let them have one of his real eyes to cure his majesty's disorder, if they would but carry him back to the spot where he had buried them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 3 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: Marvelling much at the rabbit's courtesy, the fishes slunk away into the corners for very shame at their own rude conduct in forcibly kidnapping him. The turtle was rather roughly commanded to carry the guest to the place designated. Once released to dig for the eyes in the sand, the rabbit shook the water from his coat, and winking at his clumsy betrayer told him to dig for the eyes himself, that he had only one pair, and those he intended to keep. With that he tore away up the mountain side, and has ever after been careful to give the turtle a wide berth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 3 (1889); not verbatim.

texts.period: Folk tale collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889); origin-legend of the enmity of cats and dogs

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 4 'The Enchanted Wine Jug', eBook #55539

summary.en: An old childless wine-seller by the ferry once gave his last drink to a weary divine stranger, who gave him a bit of amber: drop it in your jug and you will never want for drink. His wine never gave out; his deputy children, an old dog and an old cat, guarded the secret. One day the wine fails — the gem has been poured into a customer's jug — and the dog and cat organize a great search, cross the frozen river, recruit the rat guild to gnaw the soapstone tobacco-box, and retrieve the gem. On the way back, riding on the swimming dog's back, the cat laughs at the schoolchildren's jeering and drops the gem into the river; the dog dives, the cat clings, both are nearly drowned, and from that day cat spits at dog and dog barks at cat. In the end the dog spears a fish through the ice for his master, and the lost gem is found in the fish's belly — whereupon the old man, learning the amber duplicates whatever he wishes, becomes immensely wealthy.
summary.zh: 江畔老翁憐一疲客，傾壺與之。客贈琥珀一粒，投入瓶則酒不竭。老翁畜一犬一貓，相依為命。一日酒盡，蓋寶石誤入客瓶矣。犬貓結伴尋之，渡冰河，賂鼠齧石匣，卒得其寶。歸渡時，貓笑學童之譁，失口落寶於江；犬潛水取之，貓爪其背，幾皆溺。自此貓犬成讎。後犬於冰下啣魚歸獻主人，剖魚腹而寶石出焉。老翁乃知其能倍增萬物，遂成巨富。

sensitivity.note: Etiological animal tale; no living-community restriction.

passages.text: The old man had befriended a divine being in the form of a weary human traveller, to whom he gave the last drink his jug contained; and when the contents had gurgled down the stranger's throat in a long unbroken draught, the stranger gave him a trifling little thing that looked like a bit of amber, saying: 'Drop this into your jug, old man, and so long as it remains there, you will never want for a drink.' The dog and cat knew the secret, and had ever a watchful eye upon the jug.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 4 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day the news flashed around the neighborhood that the old man's supply of wine was exhausted; not a drop remained in his jug. He concluded that he must have poured the bit of amber into a customer's jug; and the dog and cat, listening attentively, puzzled their brains as to what was to be done. Their plan was adopted that very night: the cat called on the cats indoors and kept his smellers open, the dog chatted with the dogs outside, and they searched every house in the neighborhood, night after night, then extended the search across the frozen river.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 4 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: The cat at last traced the odor to a soapstone tobacco box on a high clothes-press, too fastened to open; the dog's wisdom enlisted the chief of the rat guild, who gnawed a hole through the stone, and a mouse pushed the gem out. The cat bore the treasure in his teeth mounted on the swimming dog's back; but nearing the bank a party of school-children burst into uproarious laughter at the absurd sight, the cat's merriment shook the dog into great gulps of water, and in his hearty laugh the cat dropped the precious gem into the river. The dog dove at once; the cat, sticking his claws into the dog's skin in his agony of suffocation, caused such pain that the dog missed his object and came to the surface. The cat got ashore, greatly angered, and climbed a tree, and has ever since been careful to avoid the dog — this accounts for the scarcity of cats and the popularity of dogs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 4 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: The dog dove many times in vain, and spent most of the following days on the river's bank. One day he espied a man spearing fish through a hole in the ice, grabbed a fish as it was laid down, and rushed off with it to his master, who was almost reduced to begging. When the old man slit the fish open, to his infinite joy his long-lost gem fell out of the fish's belly. Sitting down to think, the whole truth dawned upon him: he had been content to use his talisman simply to run a wine-shop, while he might have had money and everything else in abundance by simply giving the charm a chance to work — and so he eventually became immensely wealthy, for he could always duplicate anything with his piece of amber.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 4 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: Ching Yuh and Kyain Oo, the Star-Lovers

texts.period: Heavenly-lore prelude to the tale collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 5 'Ching Yuh and Kyain Oo', eBook #55539

summary.en: Ching Yuh and Kyain Oo were stars attendant upon the Sun. They fell madly in love, and, obtaining the royal permission, were married; but as the honey-moon bade fair to continue during the rest of their lives, rendering them unfit for the discharge of their duties, their master banished them — one to the farthest edge of the eastern heavens, the other to the opposite bank of the great river that divides the heavenly plains. They may meet but one short night in the year, when the bridge is completed by the crows, who carry the materials for its construction upon their heads — any one may know it, who cares to notice how bald and worn are the heads of the crows during the seventh moon. This sad meeting occurs on the night of the seventh day of the seventh moon; their grief at parting manifests itself in weeping tears so copious that the whole earth beneath is deluged with rains.
summary.zh: 秦玉與堅牛本日邊侍星也，相愛成婚，形影不離，廢其職守。天帝怒，一謫東極，一謫天河西岸。惟歲七夕烏鵲填橋，得一宵之聚。既別，悲泣成雨，人間因有霖雨之候。烏鵲頭頂為之禿，故七月烏頂皆禿。

sensitivity.note: Korean version of the East Asian Weaver-and-Cowherd (Chilseok) myth; shared Sinosphere heritage, tagged as heavenly lore.

passages.text: Ching Yuh and Kyain Oo were stars attendant upon the Sun. They fell madly in love with each other, and, obtaining the royal permission, they were married. It was to them a most happy union; but as the honey-moon bade fair to continue during the rest of their lives, rendering them unfit for the discharge of their duties, their master decided to punish them: he banished them, one to the farthest edge of the eastern heavens, the other to the extreme opposite side of the great river that divides the heavenly plains.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 5 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: They were sent so far away that it required full six months to make the journey. They could only hope to journey back and forth for the scant comfort of spending one short night in each other's company, and could cross the broad river only at the season when the great bridge is completed by the crows, who carry the materials for its construction upon their heads — as any one may know who cares to notice how bald and worn are the heads of the crows during the seventh moon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 5 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: Naturally this fond couple are always heart-broken and discouraged at being so soon compelled to part after such a brief but long-deferred meeting, and 'tis not strange that their grief should manifest itself in weeping tears so copious that the whole earth beneath is deluged with rains. This sad meeting occurs on the night of the seventh day of the seventh moon; if prevented by some untoward circumstance, the usual rainy season is withheld, and the parched earth unites in lamentation with the fond lovers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 5 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: The Fan Betrothal by the Roadside

texts.period: Story collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 5, eBook #55539

summary.en: Two childless households pray to heaven. You Tah Jung's wife dreams of a beautiful boy riding down from the North Star on a white feather fan — the attendant of the North Star, banished to earth, sent to her with the fan that will one day save both their lives; with the spring-tide a beautiful boy is born, Pang Noo. Cho Sung Noo's wife, moon-gazing for the meeting of the star-lovers, dreams of a little girl borne on five soft clouds, an attendant of the Queen of Heaven banished for mischief — she had driven the crows away and ruined the seventh-moon bridge out of a spirit of mischief; a daughter is born, Uhn Hah, the divine maiden. At ten, resting by the road, Uhn Hah meets Pang Noo on his way to school; for two oranges he writes on the fan: 'No girl was ever possessed of such incomparable graces as the beautiful Uhn Hah. I now betroth myself to her, and vow never to marry other so long as I live.' The fan closes; the characters are concealed; she puts it away unread.
summary.zh: 柳、趙二家皆乏嗣，各禱於天。柳妻夢北極星侍童乘白羽扇降，曰『謫降人間，此扇將活爾母子之命』，果生神童逢午。趙妻月下夢雲輦仙女，自言乃天帝侍女，以戲毀鵲橋致旱而被謫，遂生神女嫣夏。十歲時，逢午上塾過其地，以二橘易題扇曰：『天下之麗莫若嫣夏，吾誓終身不娶他人。』扇闔而字隱，女珍藏之。

passages.text: One night the wife of You Tah Jung fell asleep while praying, and dreamed a remarkable dream: a most beautiful boy came down to her riding upon a wonderful fan made of white feathers. 'I am the attendant of the great North Star, and because of a mistake I made I am banished to earth for a term of years, telling me to come to you and bring this fan, which will eventually be the means of saving your life and my own.' With the succeeding spring-tide a beautiful boy came to them; they called the boy Pang Noo.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 5 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: The wife of Cho Sung Noo, sitting in the moonlight gazing into the heavens hoping to witness the meeting of Ching Yuh and Kyain Oo, dreamed that the four winds were bearing to her a beautiful litter supported upon five rich, soft clouds, in which reclined a little girl far lovelier than any being she had ever dreamed of. 'I was an attendant upon the Queen of Heaven, but I have been very bad, though I meant no wrong, and I am banished to earth for a season.' When the annual union of Ching Yuh and Kyain Oo takes place, she hears them mourning because they can only see each other once a year; in a spirit of mischief she drove the crows away and ruined their bridge before they could reach each other — not counting on the drought that would occur, and the consequent suffering entailed on mortals. A daughter was really born to them, known popularly as the divine maiden.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 5 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: One day, resting by the road-side on her nurse's back, Uhn Hah was confronted by Pang Noo on his way to school. Seeing some oranges in her lap, he stepped up and spoke politely to the nurse: 'I am You Pang Noo, a lad on my way to school, and I am very thirsty; won't you ask your little girl to let me have one of her oranges?' In her confusion she gave him two oranges. 'If you will allow me I will write your name on this fan and present it to you.' He wrote: 'No girl was ever possessed of such incomparable graces as the beautiful Uhn Hah. I now betroth myself to her, and vow never to marry other so long as I live.' The fan being closed, no one read the characters, and Uhn Hah carefully put it away without examining it sufficiently close to discover the written sentiment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 5 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: Uhn Hah Refuses the General and Wins the Rock Test

texts.period: Story collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 5, eBook #55539

summary.en: Pang Noo wins the great examination and is made a Ussa, the King's disguised inspector; Uhn Hah, discovering at last the vow written on her fan, vows to be his or never marry. When a cruel general asks for her hand for his son, she refuses — 'I am already the wife of Pang Noo in my heart; kill me, if you will, but spare me this' — and the family must flee to another province, her parents dying on the road. In male disguise she is seized by Pang Noo's father the Governor for her fan, and released; an old man of the night feeds her a pill of superhuman strength; a blind man prophesies that her husband is fighting the rebels, nearly dead, but 'he will not die, for she will rescue him.' Petitioning the King for a command, she proves herself before the court: she throws a weather-worn stone over the enclosing wall as easily as two men could lift it from the ground, and whirls the General's sword into one continuous ring of burning steel, till the wicked General cowers in abject terror — and the King gives her the choicest battalion.
summary.zh: 逢午科舉奪魁，授暗察使。嫣夏始見扇上盟文，誓死不他適。大將軍為子求婚，女泣拒曰『妾心已屬逢午，寧死不從』，舉家避禍，父母道死。兄妹裝（易男裝）北行，為柳父所疑，繫獄得釋。夜遇老人賜大力丸；瞽者卜曰『夫在軍中將歿，然卿至則活』。女上書請纓，王命試其力：嫣夏擲庭前巨石踰牆，如提兩人之力；復舞劍如環，寒光繞身。王大悅，授精兵一營，命往平叛。

passages.text: Uhn Hah at last discovered the characters on the fan, and great was her surprise and delight at the message. She concluded it was a heaven-arranged union, and vowed she would be his or never marry at all. When one of His Majesty's greatest generals, who had a reputation for bravery and cruelty as well, asked to betroth his son to Cho's daughter, the girl was struck dumb: 'He has pledged himself to me, and I know he is even now coming to me. Would you ask one woman to marry two men? I am already the wife of Pang Noo in my heart. Kill me, if you will, but spare me this, I beg and entreat.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 5 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: The parents loved her too well to withstand her pleadings; they dispatched a letter declining the offer, and the General, in a towering rage, sent soldiers to arrest Mr. Cho. The honest local magistrate listened to Cho's story, believed the strange case, and bade them collect what they could and go to another province to live; in a distant hamlet the worn and discouraged parents were taken sick and passed on to join their ancestors. Uhn Hah and her old nurse donned male attire and journeyed on, till the Governor's procession passed by and the Governor, espying the peculiar feather fan, had the supposed men seized and questioned at the yamen. 'It is a family relic,' replied Uhn Hah; she would die rather than part with it, and was locked up — then dismissed with the steward's pity and a parting gift.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 5 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: Darkness overtook them at a little hut occupied by an old man reading a book, who called her by her true name, Cho Nang Jah, and said, 'I have been waiting for you and expecting you. You are soon to do great things. Never mind your hunger, but devour this pill; it will give you superhuman strength and courage.' When they awoke it was bright morning, the birds singing above them, their only shelter — the hut and the old man had disappeared entirely; she devoutly bowed in grateful acknowledgment of the gracious manifestation. At a wayside inn a blind man prophesied for the people: 'This is a woman in disguise; she is seeking for her husband, who is fighting the rebels, and searching for her. He is now nearly dead; but he will not die, for she will rescue him.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 5 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: Learning that Pang Noo had been carried captive by the rebels, Uhn Hah petitioned the King to be given a body of soldiers to punish the rebels and liberate her husband. The King bade her come before him; her beauty and dignity of carriage won attention, but the General suggested she first give some evidence of her strength and prowess. She breathed a prayer to her departed parents, remembered the promise of the pill, and seizing a large weather-worn stone that stood in an ornamental rock basin in the court, threw it over the enclosing wall as easily as two men would have lifted it from the ground. Then, taking the General's sword, she manipulated it, increasing gradually, till the movement became so rapid that the sword seemed like one continuous ring of burning steel, menacingly near the wicked General, who cowered in abject terror. His Majesty was completely captivated, and himself gave the orders for her expedition, raising her to relative rank and giving her the choicest battalion of troops.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 5 (1889); not verbatim.

title.en: Hungbu, the Swallow-King's Gourds of Plenty

texts.period: Folk tale collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 6 'Hyung Bo and Nahl Bo', eBook #55539

summary.en: In Chullado lived two brothers: rich Nahl Bo, who kept the whole inheritance and reduced his brother to abject misery, and poor Hyung Bo with his starving family in a hut of broom straw. When a roof-snake devours the swallow nestlings, Hyung binds up the broken legs of the one survivor with fish-skin splints; the bird flies south to the king of birds, and in spring returns bearing a seed engraved in gold: bury me in soft earth and give me plenty of water. The gourd-vine climbs the hut and bears four enormous gourds: out of the first step two beautiful boys with wine and a jade table — one bottle restores life to the dead, one sight to the blind, tobacco that gives speech to the dumb, wine that wards off age and death; the second gourd pours out household furniture, silk and satins; the third produces carpenters who build a fine house with courts, stables and granaries before the family can rise from the ground; the fourth yields a maiden of matchless beauty, sent by the bird king to be his concubine — and Hyung's wife, who sees only a rival, is sternly reprimanded and sent to reign in the women's quarters.
summary.zh: 全羅道有兄弟二人：兄諾夫富而吝，弟興夫貧而仁。燕為蛇所噬，興夫以魚皮裹其折足而療之。燕南歸告鳥王，春返啣金書之種，種之則瓜蔓滿屋，結四巨瓜。剖之：一瓜出二仙童，奉生死人藥酒、明目酒、啞者能言之煙與長生之酒；二瓜出金帛器物；三瓜出工匠，俄頃成大廈，牛馬僕從畢至；四瓜出絕色女子，云奉鳥王之命來為媵。興夫之妻妒而叱之，被夫所責，退居內舍。

sensitivity.note: Korean Cinderella-boys analog (Hungbu-Nolbu); no living-community restriction.

passages.text: In the province of Chullado, in Southern Korea, lived two brothers. One was very rich, the other very poor. For in dividing the inheritance, the elder brother, instead of taking the father's place and providing for the younger children, kept the whole property to himself, reducing Hyung Bo to a condition of abject misery; he had built himself a hut of broom straw so poor that when it rained they were deluged inside.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 6 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the little birds were taking their first lesson in flying, Hyung was lying on his back on the ground and saw a huge roof-snake crawl along and devour several little birds before he could arise and help them. One bird struggled from the reptile and fell, catching both legs in the meshes of a reed-blind, and hung helplessly within the snake's reach. Hyung hastily snatched it down, and with the help of his wife bound up the broken limbs, using dried fish-skin for splints, laying the little patient in a warm place, till the bird soon began to hop around the room and finally flew away to join his fellows.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 6 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: The bird paid homage to the king of birds in the bird-land beyond the frosts and related his rescue by a very poor but very kind man. His bird majesty gave the little cripple a seed engraved with fine characters in gold, denoting that the seed belonged to the gourd family. In the spring the bird dropped the seed, with a message: 'Bury me in soft earth, and give me plenty of water.' The stem shot up and climbed all over the house, blossoming into four small gourds that grew to an enormous size.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 6 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: Hyung got a saw and sawed open the first huge gourd: out of it stepped two beautiful boys, with fine bottles of wine and a table of jade set with dainty cups — the bird king's presents to the benefactor of one of his subjects. One wine would restore life to the dead; another would restore sight to the blind; one gold bottle contained tobacco which, being smoked, would give speech to the dumb, while the other gold bottle contained wine which would prevent the approach of age and ward off death. The next gourd poured out all manner of household furniture, clothing and rolls of fine silk and satin; the third produced a body of carpenters, who put up a fine house with courts and servants' quarters, stables and granaries before the family could arise from the ground; and out of the fourth stepped a maiden as beautiful as were the gifts that had preceded her, sent by the bird king to be this man's concubine. The wife grew dark in the face and ordered her away, upbraiding her husband for his greed in opening the fourth gourd; he commanded her to go at once to the women's quarters, where she should reign supreme.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 6 (1889); not verbatim.

region.zh: 全羅道諾夫宅（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Folk tale collected by H.N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889)

source.work: Horace N. Allen, Korean Tales (1889), ch. 6, eBook #55539

summary.en: Nahl Bo hears of his brother's transformation and demands the secret, then goes home to strike at all the birds he can see, breaking one bird's legs and binding them in splints to counterfeit his brother's kindness. The bird tells the king of the man's cruelty, and in spring a seed comes — and Nahlbu's vines bear twelve gourds that groan the great beams of his house. Opened one by one at a thousand cash a gourd, they disgorge: rope-dancers who demand 5,000 cash, Buddhist priests begging for their temple, paid mourners following a corpse, dancing girls who sing of the wind god and the twelve months, an acrobatic pair, a jester, yamen runners and an official announcing that Nahl Bo is now a serf owing heavy tribute, soothsayers with drums to exorcise disease-demons, blind fortune-tellers, a juggler who throws him headlong and stands him on his head, a giant who carries him off till ransomed — and at last a gourd that splits rotten with an awful stench, followed by a gale that destroys the buildings, which take fire from the kang, and the last of his property is swept forever from him. The seed that brought prosperity to the honest brother turned prosperity into ruin to the cruel, covetous Nahl Bo.
summary.zh: 諾夫聞弟驟富，忌且妬，乃效之傷燕足以邀福。燕訴於鳥王，春啣種至。蔓生十二巨瓜。剖之：一雜技班討錢、一僧眾化緣、一喪班哭屍、一歌伎獻曲、一戲班、一傀儡師，皆索金五千；一官差至，宣判諾夫為某公之奴，歲納重賦；一巫女擊鼓驅疫、一瞽者占卜、一力士倒拋諾夫、一巨人負之去，贖金乃放。最後一瓜臭不可近，烈風大作，屋焚產蕩。諾夫遂依弟之施捨度日。

passages.text: When Nahl Bo heard of the wonderful change taking place at his brother's establishment, he began to upbraid his brother with dishonest methods; Hyung Bo frankly told him how he had saved the bird from the snake and bound up its broken limbs. The covetous man insisted on having the fair maiden too, and in a rage departed, fully determined to use the secret of his brother's success for all it was worth. Going home he struck at all the birds he could see, and after killing many succeeded in catching one, and, breaking its legs, took fish-skin and bound them up in splints.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 6 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: The bird told the bird king of the man's cruelty in killing so many birds and then breaking its own legs; the king gave the little cripple a seed to present to the wicked man on its return in the spring. The vines were most luxurious, and instead of one gourd, or even four, the new vines bore twelve gourds, which grew till the great beams of his house fairly groaned under their weight. The carpenter insisted upon the enormous sum of 1,000 cash for opening each gourd.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 6 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: Out of the first came a party of rope-dancers who refused to leave until he had paid them 5,000 cash; number two yielded a body of Buddhist priests begging for their temple; the third a procession of paid mourners followed by a corpse. From the fourth came a band of dancing girls, one from each province, singing of the wind god, of the money christening placed on the roof tree of every house, of the twelve months that make the year — then demanding their pay. A jester came forth demanding expense money; yamen runners followed by an official read a paper announcing that Nahl Bo was the serf of a certain lord and must pay heavy tribute; a bevy of soothsayers came forth with drums to exorcise disease-demons; blind men offered to tell fortunes; a juggler threw him headlong over his own back, nearly breaking his neck, and stood him on his head; and a giant seized him and carried him off upon his shoulders till ransomed.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 6 (1889); not verbatim.

passages.text: The carpenter opened the last remaining gourd, and had only sawed a very little when it split open as though it were rotten, while a most awful stench arose, driving every one from the premises. This was followed by a gale of wind so severe as to destroy the buildings, which, in falling, took fire from the kang, and while the once prosperous man looked on in helpless misery, the last of his remaining property was swept forever from him. The seed that had brought prosperity to his honest, deserving brother had turned prosperity into ruin to the cruel, covetous Nahl Bo, who now had to subsist upon the charity of his kind brother, whom he had formerly treated so cruelly.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Allen, Korean Tales, ch. 6 (1889); not verbatim.
